opus-5.5.text:
I think part of it was just very practical reasoning, even as a kid. Math is one of those subjects where everything builds on everything else. If you understand the foundations early, then later on, when you hit physics, or programming, or competitions, you're not fighting the tools; you can actually think about the interesting problem itself.

And I noticed that time is the one resource you can't get back. In middle school I had some extra time and energy, and I thought: if I spend it now getting ahead on high-school math, then in high school I'll have room to explore other things, like computer science and algorithms, instead of just keeping up with the curriculum. It's like compound interest. A small investment early pays off more and more the longer you have it.

There was also a mindset piece. Learning things ahead of schedule teaches you that you don't need to wait for someone to hand you the material. You can pick up a book, work through it, get stuck, figure it out. That habit of self-directed learning turned out to matter much more than any specific theorem. Later, in research and engineering, nobody gives you a syllabus. You have to decide what's worth learning and go learn it.

Honestly, I also just enjoyed it. There's a satisfaction in solving a problem that's supposed to be "too advanced" for you. That enjoyment is what made it sustainable. If it had felt like pure sacrifice, I probably wouldn't have kept going.

r001.rationale: The candidate says studying high-school math early would free up time later to explore computer science and algorithms, and describes the early investment as paying off over time compared with just keeping up with the curriculum.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time I don't think I framed it as an "investment" at all. I was just a kid who found math fun, and the stuff they were teaching in class felt too slow. So I started pulling high-school textbooks off the shelf early, mostly out of curiosity and a bit of impatience.

Looking back, though, I'd say it paid off in a few ways I didn't anticipate.

The first is that it gave me a head start on math competitions, which in China is a pretty well-defined path. If you want to do well in competitions, you basically have to cover the standard curriculum early so you have time to go deeper into the actual competition material. Learning the high-school content early freed up those years.

The second thing, and this is the one I think matters more, is that it taught me I could learn things on my own without waiting for someone to teach them to me. That sounds small, but it's a mindset that carried through everything later: picking up programming, reading reinforcement learning papers, building systems. The content of high-school math is less important than the habit of "I don't know this yet, let me go figure it out."

And the third is just time. When I got to university, a lot of the foundational stuff felt familiar, so I could spend my energy on things I was genuinely excited about instead of catching up. That slack is what let me get into AI research relatively early.

So I'd put it this way: I didn't see it as a worthwhile investment back then. I just did it because I liked it. But if you ask me now, I'd absolutely tell a young student to do the same, not because math is magic, but because learning to teach yourself early compounds for a very long time.

r001.rationale: The response describes benefits of learning high-school math early, including freeing time for competition preparation and later interests. It does not clearly compare those returns with spending the same time drilling current material.
